Hi Andreia, David Lewis here. I heard you are giving a sixty-second pitch at the regional meeting next week, so here are three quick tips. First, open with a hook. Do not start with your name and your job title. Start with a short story or a surprising number, so the audience wants to hear more. Second, give them a simple outline: tell them you will talk about the problem, the solution and the results. Then signpost every step, with phrases like moving on to the results, or let me give you an example. Third, watch your pace. Most people speak too fast when they are nervous. Slow down, and pause after your key point. And please rehearse it out loud three times, with a timer. You know this program better than anyone. Good luck, and call me after the meeting.

Last year, one of our robotic surgeries stopped for forty minutes, because nobody on the team knew how to fix a small problem with the console. Today I'd like to talk about how we solved that. Let me start with the problem. We had a great robot, but only two nurses were fully trained on it. Moving on to the solution, we created a six-month training path, with simulation every week and a mentor for every nurse. And now the results. I want to emphasize one number: we trained forty nurses, and we have had zero long stops since March. To sum up, better training means safer surgery. Let me finish by asking for your support to open the program to two more hospitals. Thank you.

Here is how Andreia builds her sixty-second pitch. First, she opens with a hook: a short story from the operating room. Then she gives the audience a simple outline: the problem, the solution and the results. Next, she signposts each step, with phrases like moving on to the solution. After that, she emphasizes her key number and pauses. Finally, she concludes and asks for support.
